options: A cube root of a negative number
A square root of a negative number
A logarithm of 0 or a negative number

questions.text: Why is the domain of $ln x$ written $(0, ∞)$ and not $[0, ∞)$?
options: Logs are only defined for integers
questions.explain: The inside of a log must be strictly positive.

questions.text: Why is the domain of $sqrt x$ written $[0, ∞)$ with a square bracket?
options: Square roots of negatives are fine
questions.explain: Zero is allowed inside a square root.

questions.text: $∛x$ is defined for every real number $x$.
questions.explain: Cube roots of negatives are fine: $∛(-8) = -2$.

questions.text: The domain of $frac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}$ is all real numbers, because it simplifies to $x + 3$.
questions.explain: The original formula still divides by 0 at $x$ = 3. The graph has a hole there.

questions.text: ∞ can never get a square bracket.
questions.explain: ∞ is not a number you can reach or include.

questions.text: Which numbers are **not** in the domain of $frac{sqrt(x + 1)}{x(x - 2)}$?
questions.explain: Need $x ≥ -1$ (so −2 is out), $x ≠ 0$, $x ≠ 2$. −1 and 1 are fine.
Need $x^2 ≥ 1$: far from 0 on either side.
